Mutable

/MYOO-tuh-buhl/ - rhymes with suitable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mutable means prone to change; inconstant.

Case law treats 'reasonable' as mutable: what juries accepted in 1950 is not what they accept now.

Worked Example

The board game arrived with a rulebook and a promise: house rules encouraged. Within a year the family had voted in three new forfeits, retired the sand timer, and made the youngest player banker for life. Visiting cousins complain that it isn't the same game anymore; the family answers that it never was — the rules are mutable, and the voting is half the fun.

Mutable says only that change can happen; it schedules nothing. A mutable rule may sit unchanged for a decade — what matters is that nothing forbids Tuesday's vote from rewriting it. You met its opposite two units ago: immutable, the rule no vote can touch. Mutable is that word with the hinge oiled.

How Mutable Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

changeable

changeable: the plain twin

fluid

fluid: no shape ever quite holds — further along the same road

Antonyms

fixed

fixed: set in place, for now and until someone with authority moves it

unchanging

unchanging: staying exactly as it is

How Strong Is It? — adjustable → mutable → ever-shifting

adjustable vs. mutable

adjustable vs. mutable: Adjustable means a person can change it on purpose, one dial at a time; mutable runs deeper — the thing itself is open to change through and through.

ever-shifting vs. mutable

ever-shifting vs. mutable: Ever-shifting outruns mutable: a mutable thing can change yet may sit still for years; the ever-shifting one never settles at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mut

Root — mut: to change (Latin mutare)

Suffix — -able

Suffix — -able: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Mut (to change, from Latin mutare) + -able (able to be) = able to change. Mutare is one of Latin's busiest verbs in English clothing: genes mutate, sentences get commuted, and what traders swap between them is 'mutual.' Mutable is the family's plainest member: simply open to change.

Use the root in a new word: commute

Use the root in a new word: commute: The governor commuted the sentence from ten years to two — changed it for a lighter one, as mutare promises.

Word Choice

formal / reflective

Mutable notes, without alarm, that a thing is open to change — laws, tastes, borders, weather. You met its opposite two units ago: immutable, the rule no vote can touch. Where changeable can sound flighty, mutable keeps a philosopher's calm: fashion is changeable; the law itself is mutable.
